These two phrases **Shout joyfully to God, our strength** and **shout out to the God of Jacob** mean basically the same thing. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. For more information on translating parallel phrases, see the Introduction to this psalm. Alternate translation: [Shout with great joy to God who is the strength of Jacob’s descendants]

Asaph is saying what he wants the people of Israel to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about this form of speech and follow the decision of your team, here and throughout this psalm, of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that all shout joyfully to God, our strength; you should all shout out]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one who strengthens us]

nt: The pronoun **He** refers to God, and the pronoun **he** in **when he went out** refers to Joseph (representing Israel). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [God set it as a testimony in Joseph when Israel went out]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **testimony**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as something to be observed]

The name **Joseph** represents the people of Israel, particularly the tribes descended from Joseph. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [among the people of Israel]

nt: Yahweh is speaking as if Israel’s dependence on him were opening a mouth wide to be fed. This represents trusting God to provide abundantly. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. The word translated as **Open wide** is an imperative, but it communicates a condition rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a condition for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a condition. Alternate translation: [If you open wide your mouth, then I will fill it]

x.ASV: He would feed them also with the finest of the wheat; And with honey out of the rock would I satisfy thee.
x.Darby: And he would have fed them with the finest of wheat; yea, with honey out of the rock would I have satisfied thee.

nt: The pronouns **he** and **him** refer to Yahweh and Israel respectively. Even though Yahweh is speaking in the first person, he uses the third person here. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I would feed Israel]

Here, **fat** represents the best and richest portion of something. Yahweh is speaking as if the finest wheat had a rich fat. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with the finest wheat]
Yahweh is using this possessive form to describe the richest part of the wheat. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the richest part of the wheat]

The pronoun **you** marks an abrupt shift from the third person **him** earlier in the verse to the second person. Both refer to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I would satisfy them with honey from the rock]
